{{ElectionsNY}}
The '''2024 United States House of Representatives elections in New York''' were held on November 5, 2024, to elect the 26 [[U.S. representative]]s from the [[U.S. state|State]] of [[New York state|New York]], one from each of the state's 26 [[New York's congressional districts|congressional districts]]. The elections coincided with the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 U.S. presidential election]], as well as [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections|other elections]] to the House of Representatives, [[2024 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]], and various [[2024 United States elections|state and local elections]]. The primary elections were held on June 25, 2024.

[[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] flipped three seats held by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]], and a total of four from the [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections in New York|previous election]] (one of which they flipped in a [[2024 New York's 3rd congressional district special election|special election]] earlier in 2024), despite the concurrent [[2024 United States presidential election in New York|presidential election]] in the state swinging the most towards Republicans of any state in the nation.

{{Horizontal TOC|nonum=yes|limit=2}}

==2020–2024 redistricting process==
[[File:New York Congressional Districts, 119th Congress.svg|thumb|right|The new congressional districts map passed by the state legislature<br>{{maplink|from=New York's 1st congressional district (2025–).map|from2=New York's 2nd congressional district (2025–).map|from3=New York's 3rd congressional district (2025–).map|from4=New York's 4th congressional district (2023–).map|from5=New York's 5th congressional district (2023–).map|from6=New York's 6th congressional district (2025–).map|from7=New York's 7th congressional district (2025–).map|from8=New York's 8th congressional district (2025–).map|from9=New York's 9th congressional district (2025–).map|from10=New York's 10th congressional district (2025–).map|from11=New York's 11th congressional district (2023–).map|from12=New York's 12th congressional district (2023–).map|from13=New York's 13th congressional district (2023–).map|from14=New York's 14th congressional district (2025–).map|from15=New York's 15th congressional district (2025–).map|from16=New York's 16th congressional district (2025–).map|from17=New York's 17th congressional district (2025–).map|from18=New York's 18th congressional district (2025–).map|from19=New York's 19th congressional district (2025–).map|from20=New York's 20th congressional district (2025–).map|from21=New York's 21st congressional district (2025–).map|from22=New York's 22nd congressional district (2025–).map|from23=New York's 23rd congressional district (2025–).map|from24=New York's 24th congressional district (2025–).map|from25=New York's 25th congressional district (2025–).map|from26=New York's 26th congressional district (2025–).map|text=Interactive map version}}]]
Following the [[2020 United States census|2020 census]], [[New York (state)|New York]] lost one congressional seat and its Independent Redistricting Commission (I.R.C.) attempted to draw a new map. However, they could not reach an agreement on the map, and the Democratic-dominated [[Legislature|New York State Legislature]] drew their own new Congressional map. In April 2022, in the lead-up to the [[2022 midterms]], the [[New York State Court of Appeals]] struck down the map as an unconstitutional partisan [[gerrymander]] that failed to follow the proper procedures.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=April 27, 2022 |title=Court of Appeals axes new maps for Congress, NY Senate |url=https://nypost.com/2022/04/27/court-of-appeals-axes-new-maps-for-congress-ny-senate/ |access-date=August 4, 2023 |language=en-US}}</ref> The Court then appointed an Independent Special Master to create a new map.

In the [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections|2022 House election]] [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections in New York|in New York]], under the new map, the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] flipped three seats, bringing the new seat count of 15 for the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] and 11 held by Republicans.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=New York House Election Results 2022: Live Map {{!}} Midterm Races by District |url=https://www.politico.com/2022-election/results/new-york/house/ |access-date=August 4, 2023 |website=www.politico.com |language=en}}</ref> In March 2023, [[New York State Democratic Committee|New York Democrats]] challenged the new map, deeming it incorrect for the Court to draw the map, claiming that the job lies solely with the Legislature and I.R.C.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.timesunion.com/state/article/democrats-revive-ny-redistricting-case-battle-17866301.php|title=Dems revive redistricting case as battle for Congress begins in NY|author=Lyons, Brendan|date=March 30, 2023|work=Times Union}}</ref> In July 2023, an intermediate appeals court ruled that the I.R.C. must create another new map for the [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections|2024 House elections]].<ref>{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=July 13, 2023 |title=Fresh congressional New York map could boost Democrats' chances for 2024 House majority |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2023/jul/13/new-york-electoral-maps-redrawn-democrats-house-majority-2024 |access-date=August 4, 2023 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> The [[New York Republican State Committee|New York State Republicans]] challenged the ruling to the Court of Appeals, who ruled on December 12, 2023, that the maps must be redrawn by the legislature and I.R.C. for the 2024 elections.<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 13, 2023 |title=Republicans could lose seats after appeals court orders New York to redraw Congressional districts – CBS New York |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/appeals-court-orders-new-york-redraw-congressional-districts-republican-seats/ |access-date=August 4, 2023 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Fandos |first=Nicholas |date=December 12, 2023 |title=Top Court Clears Path for Democrats to Redraw House Map in New York |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/12/nyregion/new-york-redistricting-democrats.html |access-date=December 12, 2023 |website=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> On February 27, 2024, the [[New York State Legislature]] voted to reject the bipartisan map and instead favored redrawing the map for Democrats. On February 28, 2024, the state legislature passed a new map, resulting in the 3rd, 18th, and 22nd congressional districts becoming more Democratic, while the 1st became more Republican.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 28, 2024 |title=New York lawmakers approve a new congressional map giving Democrats a slight boost |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/new-york-lawmakers-approve-congressional-map-rcna140890 |access-date=February 28, 2024 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref> The map was signed by Governor [[Kathy Hochul]] on the same day.

==Overview==
In some races, candidates appeared on multiple ballot lines, with Democratic candidates often appearing on the Working Families line and Republican candidates often appearing on the Conservative line. However, they all caucus with either the Democrats or the Republicans.

{{see also|New York's 1st congressional district}}
The 1st district is based on the eastern end and [[North Shore (Long Island)|North Shore]] of [[Long Island]], including the [[Hamptons]], the [[North Fork (Long Island)|North Fork]], [[Riverhead (town), New York|Riverhead]], [[Port Jefferson]], [[Smithtown, New York|Smithtown]], and [[Huntington, New York|Huntington]], all in [[Suffolk County, New York|Suffolk County]].<ref name = validsource/> The incumbent was Republican [[Nick LaLota]], who was elected with 55.51% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT">{{cite web|url=https://www.cookpolitical.com/charts/house-charts/national-house-vote-tracker/2022|title=2022 National House Vote Tracker|access-date=December 30, 2023|website=[[The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter|Cook Political Report]]}}</ref> [[George Santos]], who was [[Expulsion from the United States Congress|expelled]] from Congress in December 2023, announced a Republican primary challenge to LaLota in this seat, announcing his run as a Republican during [[Joe Biden]]'s [[2024 State of the Union Address]].<ref name="SantosRunning"/> On March 22, 2024, Santos announced that he was withdrawing from the Republican primary and would instead run as an Independent candidate.<ref name = willrunindie/> On April 23, 2024, Santos withdrew from the race entirely.<ref name="irwin1">{{cite news |last1=Irwin |first1=Lauren |title= George Santos drops independent House bid |url= https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/4616359-george-santos-drops-independent-house-bid/ |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |date=April 23, 2024 |access-date=April 23, 2024}}</ref>

{{see also|New York's 2nd congressional district}}
The 2nd district is based on the [[South Shore (Long Island)|South Shore]] of [[Suffolk County, New York|Suffolk County]], including the towns of [[Babylon, New York|Babylon]], [[Islip, New York|Islip]], and most of [[Brookhaven, New York|Brookhaven]] all in Suffolk County, and [[Massapequa, New York|Massapequa]] in [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]]. The incumbent was Republican [[Andrew Garbarino]], who was re-elected with 60.73% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/>

{{see also|2024 New York's 3rd congressional district special election}}
{{see also|New York's 3rd congressional district}}
The 3rd district is based on the [[North Shore (Long Island)|North Shore]] of [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]], including all of the city of [[Glen Cove, New York|Glen Cove]], all of the town of [[North Hempstead]], most of the town of [[Oyster Bay (town), New York|Oyster Bay]], a small part of the town of [[Hempstead, New York|Hempstead]], and parts of Northeast [[Queens]], including the neighborhoods of [[Whitestone, Queens|Whitestone]], [[Beechhurst]], [[Little Neck]], and [[Douglaston]].<ref name = validsource>{{cite web | url=https://www.elections.ny.gov/district-map.html | title=Elected Officials & District Map &#124; New York State Board of Elections }}</ref> The incumbent was Republican [[George Santos]], who flipped the district and was elected with 53.76% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/> Santos had faced heavy calls to resign following [[George Santos#False biographical statements|revelations that he fabricated a majority of his résumé]], including from the [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]] Republican Party.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Gold |first1=Michael |last2=Ashford |first2=Grace |date=January 11, 2023 |title=George Santos Faces Calls to Resign From 4 G.O.P. Congressmen |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/01/11/nyregion/george-santos-nassau-resign.html |access-date=January 22, 2023 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

On May 10, 2023, Santos was arrested on federal charges of fraud and money laundering.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Freifeld |first1=Karen |last2=Lynch |first2=Sarah |title=Embattled US Rep George Santos arrested on fraud, money laundering charges |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-rep-santos-charged-with-fraud-money-laundering-statement-2023-05-10/ |access-date=May 10, 2023 |publisher=[[Reuters]] |date=May 10, 2023}}</ref>

On November 16, 2023, in light of the [[George Santos#House Ethics Committee|House Ethics Committee report]] finding that there was "substantial evidence" that he "violated federal criminal laws," Santos announced that he would no longer be seeking re-election.<ref name = brutal/> On December 1, Santos was expelled from Congress.<ref>{{cite news |title=House votes to expel indicted Rep. George Santos from Congress |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/george-santos-expulsion-congress-ny-house-ethics-committee-rcna127179 |access-date=December 1, 2023 |publisher=NBC News |date=December 1, 2023|author1=Wong, Scott|author2=Gregorian, Dareh|author3=Santaliz, Kate|author4=Stewart, Kyle}}</ref>

On February 13, 2024, former U.S. Representative [[Tom Suozzi]] defeated Republican nominee [[Mazi Melesa Pilip]] in the special election to finish Santos's term.<ref name = SuozziWins>{{Cite web |date=February 13, 2024 |title=Democrat Tom Suozzi wins New York race to succeed George Santos in Congress |url=https://apnews.com/article/george-santos-suozzi-pilip-special-election-be0140979ca3050921579e90507bfe1f |access-date=February 14, 2024 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref> He won election to a full term in November by 3.6%, defeating [[Mike LiPetri]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/05/us/elections/results-new-york-us-house-3.html|title=New York Third Congressional District Election Results|website=[[The New York Times]]|date=November 5, 2024 |access-date=December 15, 2024}}</ref>

{{see also|New York's 4th congressional district}}
The 4th district is based on the [[South Shore (Long Island)|South Shore]] of [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]] and is entirely within the town of [[Hempstead, New York|Hempstead]].<ref name = validsource/> The incumbent was Republican [[Anthony D'Esposito]], who flipped the district and was elected with 51.80% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/>

{{see also|New York's 16th congressional district}}
The 16th district is based in southern [[Westchester County]], including [[Yonkers]], [[White Plains, New York|White Plains]], [[New Rochelle]], and [[Rye, New York|Rye]]. It also includes [[Co-op City, Bronx|Co-op City]] in [[the Bronx]]. The incumbent was Democrat [[Jamaal Bowman]], who was re-elected with 64.30% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/> He faced a challenge in the Democratic primary from [[George Latimer (New York politician)|George Latimer]], the [[Westchester County Executive|Westchester County executive]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2024-06-13 |title=Stunner: Chappaqua's Hillary Clinton Endorses Westchester's Latimer For Congress |url=https://dailyvoice.com/new-york/chappaqua/stunner-chappaquas-hillary-clinton-endorses-westchesters-latimer-for-congress/ |access-date=2024-06-13 |website=Chappaqua Daily Voice |language=en}}</ref> Miriam Flisser was the Republican nominee.

===Democratic primary===
Incumbent U.S. Representative Jamaal Bowman, who was accused of being antisemitic and had been a frequent critic of [[Israel–United States relations|U.S. support]] for [[Israel]] amidst the [[Gaza-Israel conflict]], was challenged by pro-Israel Westchester County Executive George Latimer in the Democratic primary.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rep. Jamaal Bowman trails rival George Latimer by 17 points |url=https://nypost.com/2024/04/03/us-news/rep-jamaal-bowman-trails-rival-george-latimer-by-17-points/ |last=Campanile|first=Carl|date=April 3, 2024|access-date=April 4, 2024 |website=[[New York Post]]|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Fernandez |first=Madison |date=April 3, 2024 |title=Pro-Israel group looks to oust 2 members of 'the Squad' |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/04/03/dmfi-endorsements-latimer-bell-00150357 |access-date=April 3, 2024 |website=Politico}}</ref> ''[[The New York Times]]'' branded the contest "a marquee showcase of [the Democratic] party's divisions over the Israel-Hamas war".<ref name = Fandos>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/15/nyregion/bowman-latimer-aoc-squad.html|title = Progressive Democrats Scramble to Save One of Their Stars From Defeat|last = Fandos|first = Nicholas|date = June 15, 2024|accessdate = June 15, 2024|newspaper = [[The New York Times]]|url-access = limited}}</ref>

The primary was the most expensive House of Representatives primary in U.S. history, with over $14 million in outside spending benefiting Latimer's campaign. Much of the outside spending came from groups affiliated with the pro-Israel [[AIPAC|American Israel Public Affairs Committee]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Krieg |first1=Gregory |last2=Pazmino |first2=Gloria |date=2024-06-23 |title=The progressive left digs in for besieged New York Rep. Jamaal Bowman in Democratic primary clash |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/06/23/politics/bowman-latimer-new-york-16-primary/index.html |website=[[CNN]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Reisman |first1=Nick |last2=Mendez |first2=Rich |last3=Ngo |first3=Emily |date=June 25, 2024 |title=Jamaal Bowman is ousted in most expensive House primary ever |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/06/25/jamaal-bowman-loses-george-latimer-00164997 |access-date=June 25, 2024 |work=[[Politico]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Fandos |first=Nicholas |date=June 25, 2024 |title=Bowman Falls to Latimer in a Loss for Progressive Democrats |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/25/nyregion/bowman-latimer-house-new-york.html |access-date=June 26, 2024 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Latimer defeated Bowman, 58.59% to 41.41%.

=====By municipality=====
Latimer performed well in northern parts of the district that are suburban. Bowman received more support in the southern and urban areas of the district, such as the district's portion of [[The Bronx]] and the cities of [[Yonkers, New York|Yonkers]] and [[Mount Vernon, New York|Mount Vernon]].<ref>{{cite web |title=2024 Federal Primary |url=https://citizenparticipation.westchestergov.com/images/stories/pdfs/2024/Canvass_Federal_Primary_240625.pdf |website=Westchester County Government, NY}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Representative in Congress - Congressional District 16 |url=https://results.elections.ny.gov/contest/5580 |website=New York State Board of Elections}}</ref>

{{see also|New York's 17th congressional district}}
The 17th district is based in the [[Lower Hudson Valley]], including all of [[Rockland County|Rockland]] and [[Putnam County, New York|Putnam]] counties, northern [[Westchester County]], and a small part of [[Dutchess County]].<ref name = validsource/> The incumbent was Republican [[Mike Lawler]], who flipped the district and was elected with 50.32% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/> Lawler was opposed by Democrat Mondaire Jones, who had previously represented the 17th district.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Shapero |first=Julia |date=2023-07-05 |title=Mondaire Jones launches 2024 House bid to reclaim New York seat |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/4081331-mondaire-jones-launches-bid-to-reclaim-new-york-house-seat/ |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Working Families primary===
In a surprising twist, political enthusiast Anthony Frascone successfully rallied Rockland County voters to vote for him in the Working Families primary and defeated Democratic nominee Mondaire Jones. Aside from Frascone's effort, the turnout for the primary in Westchester, Putnam and Dutchess was almost entirely non-existent.<ref name=wf17>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/05/nyregion/mondaire-jones-bowman-wfp.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share&referringSource=articleShare | title=How a New York Democrat Lost a Progressive Ballot Line to a G.O.P. Proxy | work=The New York Times | last1=Fandos | first1=Nicholas | date=July 5, 2024 }}</ref> Following Frascone's primary win, Working Families Party leaders called him a fake candidate and accused him of having stolen the party's ballot line to help Republican Mike Lawler win the general election.<ref name=wfpprimary /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cityandstateny.com/politics/2024/10/wfp-launches-new-attack-ad-against-wfp-candidate/400666/|title=WFP launches new attack ad against WFP candidate|date=October 30, 2024|website=City & State NY}}</ref>

====Nominee====
*Anthony Frascone<ref name="surprise">{{cite web|url=https://results.elections.ny.gov/contest/5566|title=2024 Jun 25 - Working Families Primary Results - Representative in Congress - Congressional District 17|website=elections.ny.gov|access-date=July 1, 2025}}</ref>

====Eliminated in primary====
*[[Mondaire Jones]], member of the [[U.S. Commission on Civil Rights]] and former U.S. representative (2021–2023)<ref name="boomerang" /><ref name="surprise" />

{{see also|New York's 18th congressional district}}
The 18th district is based in the mid-[[Hudson Valley]], including all of [[Orange County, New York|Orange County]] and most of [[Dutchess County|Dutchess]] and [[Ulster County|Ulster]] counties.<ref name = validsource/> The incumbent was Democrat [[Pat Ryan (politician)|Pat Ryan]], who was re-elected with 50.67% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/>

{{see also|New York's 19th congressional district}}
The 19th district stretches from the [[Upper Hudson Valley]] across the [[Catskill Mountains]] to parts of the [[Southern Tier]] and [[Finger Lakes]], including [[Hudson, New York|Hudson]], [[Monticello, New York|Monticello]], [[Oneonta, New York|Oneonta]], [[Binghamton]], and [[Ithaca, New York|Ithaca]]. It includes all of [[Columbia County, New York|Columbia]], [[Greene County, New York|Greene]], [[Sullivan County, New York|Sullivan]], [[Delaware County, New York|Delaware]], [[Otsego County, New York|Otsego]], [[Chenango County, New York|Chenango]], [[Broome County, New York|Broome]], and [[Tompkins County, New York|Tompkins]] counties, and parts of [[Rensselaer County, New York|Rensselaer]], [[Cortland County, New York|Cortland]], and [[Ulster County|Ulster]] counties. The incumbent was Republican [[Marc Molinaro]], who flipped the district and was elected with 50.78% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/>

{{see also|New York's 20th congressional district}}
The 20th district is based in the [[Capital District (New York)|Capital Region]], including [[Albany, New York|Albany]], [[Troy, New York|Troy]], [[Schenectady]], [[Saratoga Springs]], and [[Amsterdam, New York|Amsterdam]]. It includes all of [[Albany County, New York|Albany]] and [[Schenectady County|Schenectady]] counties, and parts of [[Saratoga County|Saratoga]], [[Rensselaer County|Rensselaer]], and [[Montgomery County, New York|Montgomery]] counties. The incumbent was Democrat [[Paul Tonko]], who was re-elected with 55.07% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/>

{{see also|New York's 21st congressional district}}
The 21st district is based in the [[North Country (New York)|North Country]] and [[Adirondack Mountains]], including [[Glens Falls, New York|Glens Falls]], [[Lake George (town), New York|Lake George]], [[Plattsburgh, New York|Plattsburgh]], [[Potsdam, New York|Potsdam]], [[Herkimer, New York|Herkimer]], and [[Rome, New York|Rome]]. The incumbent was Republican [[Elise Stefanik]], who was re-elected with 59.1% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/>

{{see also|New York's 22nd congressional district}}
The 22nd district is based in [[Central New York]] and the [[Mohawk Valley]], including [[Syracuse, New York|Syracuse]] and [[Utica, New York|Utica]]. It includes all of [[Onondaga County, New York|Onondaga]] and [[Madison County, New York|Madison]] counties, and parts of [[Oneida County, New York|Oneida]], [[Cayuga County, New York|Cayuga]], and [[Cortland County, New York|Cortland]] counties. The incumbent was Republican [[Brandon Williams (politician)|Brandon Williams]], who was elected with 50.49% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/>

Challenger Mannion defeated incumbent Williams by a larger-than-expected 9.2% margin. After Mannion was sworn-in on January 3, 2025, this marked the first time the city of Syracuse was congressionally represented by a Democrat in 10 years.

{{see also|2024 New York's 26th congressional district special election}}
{{see also|New York's 26th congressional district}}
The 26th district is based in the Buffalo-Niagara Falls area, including the more urban parts of Erie County and western Niagara County. The incumbent was Democrat [[Brian Higgins]], who was re-elected with 63.94% of the vote in 2022.<ref name="HPVT"/> Higgins resigned on February 2, 2024, to become president of [[Shea's Performing Arts Center]].<ref name="Zremski 2024">{{cite web|url=https://buffalonews.com/news/local/brian-higgins-to-leave-congress-on-friday/article_01473b76-bd17-11ee-98db-9f2414cd3a97.html|title=Brian Higgins to leave Congress on Friday|last=Zremski|first=Jerry|date=January 27, 2024|access-date=January 28, 2024|website=[[The Buffalo News]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240204050758/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/brian-higgins-to-leave-congress-on-friday/article_01473b76-bd17-11ee-98db-9f2414cd3a97.html|archive-date=February 4, 2024|url-status=dead}}</ref>
